turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr. Hale, come on through. I'll grab a blood pressure and a pulse before the doctor sees you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. I hope I have not kept anyone waiting.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Pressure is one forty-two over eighty-eight. Let me repeat that, you just sat down. One thirty-six over eighty-two. Pulse is seventy-eight.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I did come up the stairs rather quickly. The second reading is probably the fairer one.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): She's finishing a note, then she'll be right in.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mr. Hale, thanks for waiting. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I have come about pain in my stomach, Doctor, and I have also been sleeping poorly. I felt it was time to have someone look at it.
[SEG0008] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Ruth. I live in with him, and I drove. Traffic on Maple was a mess, by the way, we circled the lot twice.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Glad you made it. Ruth, I'll want your view too. Mr. Hale, where is the pain, and what is it like?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It is a burning pain in the upper part of my stomach, moderately uncomfortable. It comes most days, particularly after I eat, and a little purple pill takes the edge off.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have you had it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): About two weeks. Forgive me, that is not correct. It is closer to five weeks, though I cannot give you the exact date it began.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Most days for about five weeks, burning, after meals. Any vomiting with it?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have not vomited at all.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, black stools, or chest pain?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, no black stools, and no chest pain. I am quite certain of that.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Regarding the pill, I have been taking a little purple pill for heartburn, once a day. The dose is, um, maybe twenty milligrams. I am not certain of the number, and I never learned the proper name.
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And he doesn't take it every morning. Some days I find it still sitting in the Monday slot on Wednesday.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right. A little purple heartburn pill, possibly twenty milligrams, once a day, not always actually swallowed, name unknown. We'll leave it described that way.
[SEG0020] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's lost weight, too. His good trousers hang on him.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I must respectfully disagree. I do not believe I have lost any weight. It has been steady.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll hold both of those and not pretend we weighed him today. Tell me about the sleep.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I lie awake a good deal, and the burning often wakes me. I would say the poor sleep has gone on for about two weeks.
[SEG0024] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Longer. It's been at least two months. He's in the kitchen at two in the morning, lights on, just standing there.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): So two weeks from you, Mr. Hale, and at least two months from Ruth. I'll call it somewhere between two weeks and two months, since you don't agree on a number.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): That is a fair summary. I simply had not counted the earlier nights.

[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud here. Burning after meals, a heartburn pill that helps a little, this may be gastritis or acid reflux. I was going to suggest an over-the-counter antacid and skip blood tests. Before I settle on that, do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Only socially.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Socially covers a wide range. What does a usual evening look like?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. I did not mean to be evasive a moment ago.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Yeah. It's the bottle with dinner, not a splash in a glass. He corks it and it's gone.

[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): I appreciate you saying it straight. I'm not going to lecture you. A bottle most nights does change the plan I just sketched, because wine can inflame the stomach and it can stress the liver.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Please tell me what you would advise.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me examine you first. Your abdomen is soft. There is mild tenderness in the upper middle, the epigastrium. No guarding and no rebound, and I can hear bowel sounds.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that spot is tender under your hand.
[SEG0036] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He flinched. I saw it.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): I had also been considering an ultrasound this afternoon. Soft belly, no fever, I'm setting that aside. My impression is gastritis or acid reflux, possibly stirred up by the wine. Not confirmed, just the best fit so far.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): An ultrasound did sound rather involved for a stomach ache.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Instead I'll order liver blood tests, a hepatic panel with the enzymes and bilirubin, because of the wine and this upper abdominal pain. For the pain I was going to start omeprazole at forty milligrams. Thinking it through, twenty milligrams is the better starting dose.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Would that be by mouth? And shall I keep taking the purple pill beside it?

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): By mouth, twenty milligrams every morning before breakfast, for the stomach pain. Leave the purple pill off while you are on the omeprazole, so we are not stacking two acid medicines.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Very well. I will set the purple one aside.

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you can bring the wine down from a bottle toward a glass, or skip some nights, that will help both the stomach and the liver. No scolding in that, just how the organs work.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall try. The evenings are quiet, and the wine has become a habit I am not proud of. There is a biography on the nightstand I keep meaning to finish instead.
[SEG0045] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I can put the bottle in the cupboard instead of on the counter. That helps a little, sometimes.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back in two weeks to go over those blood results and see if the omeprazole is doing its job. If the pain turns severe, or you vomit blood, or your skin turns yellow, do not wait for that appointment. Go to the emergency room.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. You have explained it clearly, and I am grateful.

spec.situation: Person attending for stomach pain and poor sleep; alcohol answered casually ('socially'), later 'a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps'; doctor non-judgemental; liver blood tests ordered; stomach medicine started.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

bad.reason: Dose is uncertain 'maybe twenty milligrams' and caregiver says not consistently taken, so current use detail is uncertain.
bad.text: little purple pill (dose=20 mg, frequency=once a day, indication=heartburn, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

Doctor stated they would review the blood test results at the follow-up visit in two weeks.
Doctor considered but then decided against an ultrasound this afternoon based on soft abdomen and no fever.
